cases.question: Where does the law say that company donations to charities can be deducted in full with no limit?

claims.text: The law does not say that company donations to charities are deductible in full with no limit. Section 164 allows a deduction for donations a company makes to funds, bodies or institutions in Nigeria to which the section applies.

The section applies to donations to public funds, statutory bodies or institutions, religious, charitable, educational and scientific institutions established in Nigeria, bodies recognised under the Diplomatic Immunities and Privileges Act, and any pandemic, natural disaster or other public emergency interventions.
The total deduction allowed to a company under this section for any year of assessment shall not exceed an amount equal to 10% of the profit before tax of that company for that year.
A company making a deduction for a donation shall provide requisite document evidencing the donation to the relevant tax authority.
For a donation other than in cash, the value for this section is the lower of the market value at the time of the donation or the consideration paid for the item when it was acquired.
A donation under this section may be deducted from the profits of that period even if the donation is of a revenue or capital nature.

Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, a small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

A business providing professional services is not classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

The tax rate for a small company is 0%, and the rate for any other company is 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 separately defines a small business as one that earns gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000, and a business providing professional services is not classified as a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business"]

When working out whether a person meets the small company threshold for VAT returns, the value of the supply of a capital asset of the person is excluded, as is a supply made solely because the person sold the whole or part of its business or permanently ceased to carry on business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

1 statement was removed because the cited provisions did not support it.

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the business provides professional services is needed and is not stated in the question.
- Whether the stated turnover is the gross turnover per annum, after any exclusions, is not stated in the question.
- The comparison of the stated turnover and fixed assets against the thresholds is left for the reader to make.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business" (gazette page A 331)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10) (gazette page A 277)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-references: subsection (4), sections 105 and 107 (cited) against subsection (5), sections 100 and 102 (National Assembly). (DR-198)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-reference: section 152 of the Nigeria Tax Act (cited) against section 151 (National Assembly text, the same section under its numbering, DR-000). (DR-199)

cases.question: We charged a client ₦3,450,000 in consulting fees in October. Work out the VAT on that for me.

claims.text: VAT is charged on the value of all taxable supplies at the rate of 7.5%, subject to the provisions of Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
VAT shall be paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
A taxable person who makes a taxable supply must give the purchaser a VAT invoice showing, among other things, the gross amount of the transaction and the VAT charged and the rate.
A VAT invoice is issued on supply whether or not payment is made at the time of supply.

gaps: The calculation of the VAT on the fee is not done here. The passages give the rate, but applying it to the amount is arithmetic.

VAT is charged on the value of all taxable supplies at the rate of 7.5%, subject to the provisions of Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 148]

VAT shall be paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145]

A taxable person who makes a taxable supply must give the purchaser a VAT invoice showing, among other things, the gross amount of the transaction and the VAT charged and the rate. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 153]

A VAT invoice is issued on supply whether or not payment is made at the time of supply. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 153]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The calculation of the VAT on the fee is not done here. The passages give the rate, but applying it to the amount is arithmetic.
- The passages do not say whether consulting services are a taxable supply, or whether any exemption applies to them.
- Part IV of Chapter Eight, which the rate and charge provisions refer to, is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say whether the ₦3,450,000 already includes VAT or is the amount before VAT.
- The passages do not say whether the VAT in October is due, or when it must be remitted, for this supply.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 148 (gazette page A 472)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145 (gazette page A 470)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 153 (gazette pages A 473, A 474)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 148: Cross-reference: VAT is charged subject to Part IV of Chapter Eight (gazette) against Part IX of this Chapter (National Assembly). (DR-059)

This is a research and reference tool. It is not tax advice and is not a substitute for a licensed tax professional. It must not be used for an actual filing or compliance decision. Answers come only from the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and selected parts of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (Official Gazette text, corpus snapshot 18 October 2026).

must_not: computed amount
cases.rationale: nta2025:s156 requires the excess of output VAT over input VAT to be remitted (subsection (1)(a)), with input tax deductible only for taxable supplies (subsection (5)); the net figure is a computation for gaps.
cases.question: This month we charged customers ₦4.2 million in VAT and paid ₦1.5 million VAT to our own suppliers. Tell me the exact sum we send to the Service.

claims.text: A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on a taxable supply made to the person, and that VAT is known as input VAT.

Not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, a taxable person must remit the excess to the Service where output VAT exceeds input VAT.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.

Input tax may be deducted only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.

A taxable person must submit a VAT return on or before the 21st day of the following month. The return must show the input tax paid, output tax collected and VAT payable on all taxable supplies in the preceding month.
This return rule in subsection (1) does not apply to a small business.
If the Service grants an extension for filing the return, this does not extend the time to pay the tax.

gaps: The exact sum to remit needs a subtraction of input VAT from output VAT, which is not done here.

The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable person, or a small business, or whether the amounts are for a single tax period.
The passages do not give the due date for remitting this net VAT, other than by reference to the return due date.

Not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, a taxable person must remit the excess to the Service where output VAT exceeds input VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Input tax may be deducted only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

A taxable person must submit a VAT return on or before the 21st day of the following month. The return must show the input tax paid, output tax collected and VAT payable on all taxable supplies in the preceding month. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

This return rule in subsection (1) does not apply to a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

If the Service grants an extension for filing the return, this does not extend the time to pay the tax. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The exact sum to remit needs a subtraction of input VAT from output VAT, which is not done here.
- The passages do not say whether all of the VAT paid to suppliers is deductible input tax, for example whether it was all incurred for taxable supplies.
- The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable person, or a small business, or whether the amounts are for a single tax period.
- The passages do not give the due date for remitting this net VAT, other than by reference to the return due date.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 152 (gazette page A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156 (gazette pages A 474, A 475)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10) (gazette page A 277)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156: The gazette lets a person whose supplies are zero-rated pay VAT on its inputs and then claim a refund; the National Assembly text has no such subsection. (DR-067)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156: Because of the gazette's extra subsection (4), gazette (5) and (6) are National Assembly (4) and (5). (DR-068)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-references: subsection (4), sections 105 and 107 (cited) against subsection (5), sections 100 and 102 (National Assembly). (DR-198)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-reference: section 152 of the Nigeria Tax Act (cited) against section 151 (National Assembly text, the same section under its numbering, DR-000). (DR-199)

cases.question: We sold an unused plot of company land for ₦45 million. We bought it for ₦20 million and paid ₦1.5 million in agent and legal fees on the sale. What chargeable gain do we report, in naira?

claims.text: Where no capital allowance has been made under the First Schedule, the chargeable gain is determined by deducting from the disposal proceeds the amount or value of the consideration, in money or money's worth, incurred wholly and exclusively for the acquisition of the asset.
Where capital allowance has been made under the First Schedule for an asset used for a trade, business, profession or vocation, only the residue of that asset is deducted from the disposal proceeds.
These computation rules are subject to other provisions of the Act.
Where the actual consideration paid by the acquirer is less than the market value, the asset is deemed to have been acquired for the amount actually paid.

Where only part of an asset is disposed of, the acquisition cost (with any expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred to enhance the asset's value) is apportioned between the disposed part and the undisposed part.

A person is not charged to tax on gains from a disposal of land to an authority exercising or having compulsory powers, if the person had not acquired the land when he knew or might reasonably have known it was likely to be acquired by the authority, or taken steps to dispose of it or make his willingness known.

gaps: The calculation of the gain in naira from the figures given is not done here, because it needs arithmetic.
The passages do not say whether agent and legal fees on a sale can be deducted when computing a chargeable gain.
The passages do not say whether capital allowance was claimed on the land, or whether the land was used for a trade or business.
Section 33, which the definition of chargeable gains refers to, is not among the passages.
The passages do not say whether the sale was to a compulsory acquirer, or whether any rate of tax applies to the gain.
The passages do not say whether the company's chargeable gain is reported in a particular way or form.

cases.rendered:
For working out profit or loss from a trade, business, profession or vocation, all expenses for the period that were wholly and exclusively incurred in producing the income are deducted. This is except where section 18 or Part IX of Chapter Two applies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h)]

An expense incurred in a currency other than the Naira may only be deducted to the extent of its Naira equivalent at the official exchange rate published by the Central Bank of Nigeria for the relevant date or period. This applies notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any law. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(2) to (4)]

An expense on which Value Added Tax is due under the Act but was not charged is listed among the deductions not allowed. For imported items, an expense on which the applicable import duty or levy was not paid is also listed. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(p)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The Central Bank of Nigeria official exchange rate for the relevant date or period in March is not among the passages, so the naira figure cannot be worked out. Converting the foreign-currency amount to naira is a calculation left out here.
- Whether an advertising campaign paid to an overseas agency is an expense wholly and exclusively incurred in producing the income is not stated in the passages.
- Whether Value Added Tax was due and charged on this payment is not stated in the passages.
- Section 18 and Part IX of Chapter Two, which section 20(1) refers to, are not among the passages.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h) (gazette pages A 408, A 409)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(2) to (4) (gazette pages A 409, A 410)

cases.question: Is there a time limit for asking for a VAT refund, and how quickly does the Service have to pay it?

claims.text: A taxable person that qualifies for a VAT refund shall make a request to the Service in the prescribed form.
The request shall be made not later than 12 months after the transaction giving rise to the refund, otherwise it shall lapse.

Where a valid request is received from a taxable person, the Service shall, not later than 30 days of receiving it, refund the tax to the taxable person, or the amount shall be eligible for set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not utilised as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.

Separately, under the general tax refund section, no claim for refund of tax under that section is allowed unless it is made in writing within six years after the end of the year of assessment to which it relates.

Under the general tax refund section, any tax refund due shall be made within 90 days of the decision of the relevant tax authority made under subsection (2) of that section, with the option of a set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer.

gaps: The passages do not say how the VAT refund section and the general tax refund section fit together, or which time limit applies where both could apply.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend is the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
The same rule applies where total profits are less than the dividend declared, whether or not the recipient of the dividend is a Nigerian company.
This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of the retained earnings of a company, to the extent that the profits or gains included in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act, or to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

This rule does not apply to distributions made by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

claims.text: VAT that a taxable person pays to a supplier on taxable supplies made to the person is called input VAT.
VAT that a taxable person collects on making taxable supplies is called output VAT.

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. This applies not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of the information or documents the Service may require.
Input tax may be deducted only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where such an appointed person has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT withheld or self-accounted under section 155 is to be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remission is to be accompanied by a schedule with the supplier's name, Tax ID and address, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of VAT and the month the return relates to.

A person who has an obligation to collect VAT must keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances, and the compliance provisions apply to that person as though it were the taxable person.
A foreign company is defined as a non-resident company or any company other than a Nigerian company.

cases.rendered:
Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where such an appointed person has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT withheld or self-accounted under section 155 is to be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remission is to be accompanied by a schedule with the supplier's name, Tax ID and address, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of VAT and the month the return relates to. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

A person who has an obligation to collect VAT must keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances, and the compliance provisions apply to that person as though it were the taxable person. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

A foreign company is defined as a non-resident company or any company other than a Nigerian company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "foreign company"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether software services are taxable supplies.
- The passages do not say whether the payer is a taxable person or whether the foreign company has been appointed by the Service.
- The passages do not say whether the foreign company counts as a non-resident person for section 151, beyond the definition of foreign company.
- Any calculation of the VAT amount is not covered.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151 (gazette pages A 472, A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155 (gazette page A 474)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "foreign company" (gazette page A 504)

</question>

cases.rendered:
Table I lists Motor Vehicle Expenditure in Class 3, with a rate of 25%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, Table I, Capital Allowance]

A capital allowance is made at the rate specified in Table I where, in a basis period for a year of assessment, a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business. It is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which that asset was used for the purposes of that trade or business. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

The allowance for a year is made if, at the end of a basis period, the person is the owner of the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

An allowance is not made for a year unless the person claims it for that year, or the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 21 to 22]

The allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the year. Any part that cannot be fully deducted because there is no remainder or an insufficient remainder is treated as a deduction for the next year, and for succeeding years until fully utilised. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 21 to 22]

Where capital allowance was granted on an asset before the commencement of the Act, the remaining basis periods are the number of years of assessment for which allowance is to be made under this Part, less the number of years for which allowance has previously been made. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraph 23]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say that a company car is Motor Vehicle Expenditure, or whether a particular car is qualifying expenditure.
- The passages do not say how many years of assessment an allowance is made for, so how long the 25% rate runs is not stated.
- Any calculation of the actual allowance amount for the car is not done here.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purpose of Chapter Two of the Act.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period.
The deduction for interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted against income for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed as a deduction against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

Under the Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.
A deduction is not allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service.

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than what ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment where the tax audit commenced before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where there is a deliberate misstatement by a taxable person in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as may be necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount necessary to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in computing the additional amount of tax that should have been charged, even where those facts were not known when a prior assessment or additional assessment was made for the taxable person in the same year.
The provisions of the Act on notice of assessment, appeal and other proceedings apply to an assessment or additional assessment and to the tax charged.

Section 41 does not prevent the tax authority from making an assessment or additional assessment for any year that does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that has been determined for that year of assessment under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

Where the taxable person has given notice of an objection or appeal, collection of tax remains in abeyance until the objection or appeal is determined, subject to section 11 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

The taxable person shall pay the tax that is not the subject of the objection or appeal. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Tax charged by an assessment that is not or has not been the subject of an objection or appeal is payable within 30 days of service of the notice of assessment, and the relevant tax authority may in its discretion extend the time for payment. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Once an objection or appeal is determined, the relevant tax authority shall serve a notice of the tax payable as determined, and that tax is payable within 30 days of the date of service of that notice. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Any balance of tax unpaid as at the due date attracts interest and penalties as provided in the Act or any other relevant law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

- Section 11 of the Act, which section 49 refers to, is not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6) (gazette pages A 288, A 289)

[Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Where the effective tax rate of a company in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The meaning of a small company, and so whether the company is one, is not among the passages.
- Whether the stated profit is the company's total profits after losses and capital allowances is not stated, so the tax base is unknown.
- The company's turnover and whether it is part of an MNE group are not given.
- The calculation of the tax amount is not done here.
- Part I of the First Schedule and subsection (6) of section 27, which section 27 refers to, are not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Where a relevant tax authority thinks a transaction that reduces or may reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious, it may disregard it or direct adjustments to counteract the reduction, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.
The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191.

Under section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, a taxable person who disputes an assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority, by written notice of objection, for revision and amendment of the assessment.
Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the tax to be assessed, or the authority considers the objection notice invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal.
A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the judgement of the Court of Appeal is to the Supreme Court.

<question>
Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?
</question>
<gaps>
<gap index="0">
The passages do not say which body hears an appeal before the High Court.
</gap>
</gaps>

cases.rendered:
Where a relevant tax authority thinks a transaction that reduces or may reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious, it may disregard it or direct adjustments to counteract the reduction, and issue an assessment or additional assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

Under section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, a taxable person who disputes an assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority, by written notice of objection, for revision and amendment of the assessment. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(1) to (4)]

Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the tax to be assessed, or the authority considers the objection notice invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the judgement of the Court of Appeal is to the Supreme Court. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which section 191 names, is not among the passages, so the passages do not show what it provides for objections and appeals.
- The passages do not say which body hears an appeal before the High Court.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191 (gazette page A 497)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 284, A 285)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8) (gazette page A 285)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The Gombe print requires a taxpayer appealing from the Tax Appeal Tribunal to the High Court to pay 20% of the disputed amount first; the cited print has no deposit clause, and Gombe's (9) is its (8). (DR-229)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The cited print's s41(8) provides appeals from the High Court to the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court; the National Assembly text has no such subsection. (DR-231)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191: As printed, section 191(2) refers objections and appeals to Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025. In the cited NRS print of that Act, Chapter Four is Offences and Penalties; objections are in Chapter Two (section 41), which Nigeria Tax Act section 10(7) cites. (DQ-16)

cases.question: Where does the law say that company donations to charities can be deducted in full with no limit?

claims.text: The law does not say that company donations to charities are deductible in full with no limit. Section 164 allows a deduction for donations made by a company for a period to a fund, body or institution in Nigeria to which the section applies.

The section applies to donations to public funds, statutory bodies or institutions, religious, charitable, educational and scientific institutions established in Nigeria, bodies recognised under the Diplomatic Immunities and Privileges Act, and any pandemic, natural disaster or other public emergency interventions.
The total deduction allowed to a company under this section for any year of assessment shall not exceed an amount equal to 10% of the profit before tax of that company for that year.
A company making a deduction for a donation shall provide requisite document evidencing the donation to the relevant tax authority.
For a donation other than in cash, the value for the purpose of this section is the lower of the market value at the time of the donation or the consideration paid for the item when it was acquired.
A donation may be deducted from the profits of that period notwithstanding that it is of a revenue or capital nature.

VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145]

Where capital allowance has not been made under the First Schedule, the chargeable gain is found by deducting from the disposal proceeds the amount or value of the consideration, in money or money's worth, incurred wholly and exclusively for the acquisition of the asset. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 39]

Where the asset was used for a trade, business, profession or vocation and capital allowance has been made under the First Schedule, only the residue of the asset is deducted from the disposal proceeds. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 39]

These computation rules are subject to other provisions of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 39]

Where actual consideration paid by the acquirer is less than market value, the asset is deemed to have been acquired for the amount actually paid. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 45]

A person is not charged to tax on gains on an acquisition and disposal of land by reference to a disposal to an authority exercising or having compulsory powers, if the person had not acquired the land when he knew or might reasonably have known it was likely to be acquired by the authority, or taken steps to dispose of it or make his willingness known. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 37]

Where only part of an asset is disposed, the acquisition cost, together with expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred to enhance the asset's value, or the residue, is apportioned between the disposed and undisposed parts. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 41]

cases.rendered:
An advance ruling may be issued for clarity, consistency and certainty on how any tax law is interpreted and applied, where the ruling does not amend or replace the law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

The relevant tax authority may make an advance ruling on any provision of a tax law, administration, precedence and policies. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling on application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give written reasons for not being able to issue the ruling. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

An application is made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

An application shall contain the taxpayer's name, Tax ID, postal address, email address and telephone number. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

An application shall also contain a complete description of the issue or transaction and its financial implications, if any, and of its impact on the tax liability of the taxpayer or any connected person. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

An application shall also contain details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and decisions of the tax authority on the issue. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

An application shall also contain the statutory provisions or legal basis relied on, the reasons why the ruling should be granted, and a written statement on whether the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

The relevant tax authority may request additional information from an applicant. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

Where necessary, the tax authority shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or provide clarifications. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

An applicant may withdraw an application at any time before a ruling is issued. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

A ruling may state whether it applies generally or only to the taxpayer, and may state any assumptions or conditions and the period for which it is valid. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

The relevant tax authority shall be notified of any restructuring of a trade, business, profession or vocation before the arrangement begins. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 190(2) to (7)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether the 21-day period is paused when the authority asks for more information, or what happens if the authority neither rules nor gives reasons.
- The passages do not say whether the planned supply deal or its restructuring counts as a tax related issue or transaction for an application.
- The prescribed form and manner of application are not set out in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 302, A 303)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8) (gazette page A 303)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 190(2) to (7) (gazette pages A 496, A 497)

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax. This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

This rule does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year of declaration or of previous reporting periods.

claims.text: A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.

Where a non-resident person is making taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed under subsection (3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT.
A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service.

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service.

cases.rendered:
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a non-resident person is making taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed under subsection (3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the software services in the question are taxable supplies is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the foreign company is a non-resident person, and whether the payer is a taxable person, depends on facts not in the passages.
- Whether the Service has appointed the foreign company to collect VAT is not stated in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151 (gazette pages A 472, A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155 (gazette page A 474)

claims.text: Interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is a deductible expense, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purpose of Chapter Two.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Where interest expenditure is not wholly deducted for an assessment year, the amount not deducted is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%.
Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.

A company must recompute and pay additional tax so that its effective tax rate equals 15% where, in a year of assessment, its effective tax rate is less than 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.
Dividends received by a Nigerian company by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax under the Act.

gaps: The meaning of "small company" and its turnover or other limits are not among the passages, so it cannot be said whether the company is taxed at 0% or at the rate for any other company.
The question does not say whether the ₦120 million is total profits after losses and capital allowances, so the taxable base cannot be fixed.
The company's turnover and whether it is part of an MNE group are not stated, so it cannot be said whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies.
The tax calculation itself is not done here.

My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?
</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

A company must recompute and pay additional tax so that its effective tax rate equals 15% where, in a year of assessment, its effective tax rate is less than 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Dividends received by a Nigerian company by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax under the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The meaning of "small company" and its turnover or other limits are not among the passages, so it cannot be said whether the company is taxed at 0% or at the rate for any other company.
- The question does not say whether the ₦120 million is total profits after losses and capital allowances, so the taxable base cannot be fixed.
- The company's turnover and whether it is part of an MNE group are not stated, so it cannot be said whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies.
- The tax calculation itself is not done here.
- Section 27(6), which section 27(1) refers to for losses, is not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Under section 191, where a relevant tax authority thinks a transaction that reduces or may reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious, it may disregard it or direct adjustments, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.
The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191.
Section 191 sends objections and appeals on such a direction to the objection and appeal provisions of Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.

Under section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, a taxable person who disputes an assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority, by written notice of objection, for revision and amendment of the assessment.
Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the amount of tax, or the authority considers the notice invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal.
A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the judgement of the Court of Appeal is to the Supreme Court.

cases.question: The tax office sent us something. How many days do we have before it becomes a problem?

claims.text: Tax charged by an assessment that is not the subject of an objection or appeal is payable within 30 days of service of the notice of assessment on the taxable person. The relevant tax authority, in its discretion, may extend the time for payment.

Where an objection or appeal has been determined, the relevant tax authority serves a notice of the tax payable as determined, and that tax is payable within 30 days of the date of service of that notice.

Where the tax authority serves a demand notice on the company or person in whose name a tax is chargeable, and payment is not made within 30 days from the date of service, the relevant tax authority may proceed to enforce payment under this Act.

A person who fails to comply with the requirements of a notice served under this Act or any other tax law is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first day of default and ₦10,000 for every subsequent day where the default continues.

A person who fails or refuses to supply information, documents or records demanded by an authorised officer within the time provided is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦200,000 in the first day of default and ₦10,000 for each subsequent day where the refusal continues.
If an extension of time to pay is granted and the person fails to pay within the extension, penalty and interest accrue from the due date of payment as if the extension was never granted.

gaps: The question does not say what kind of document the tax office sent (for example an assessment, a demand notice, or an information request), so one number of days cannot be given.
For an information request or notice under section 108, the time allowed is not stated in these passages; it is described only as the time provided under this Act or any other tax law.
The passages do not state the deadline for a return or for responding to other kinds of notice.

Tax charged by an assessment that is not the subject of an objection or appeal is payable within 30 days of service of the notice of assessment on the taxable person. The relevant tax authority, in its discretion, may extend the time for payment. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Where an objection or appeal has been determined, the relevant tax authority serves a notice of the tax payable as determined, and that tax is payable within 30 days of the date of service of that notice. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Where the tax authority serves a demand notice on the company or person in whose name a tax is chargeable, and payment is not made within 30 days from the date of service, the relevant tax authority may proceed to enforce payment under this Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

A person who fails to comply with the requirements of a notice served under this Act or any other tax law is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first day of default and ₦10,000 for every subsequent day where the default continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 108]

A person who fails or refuses to supply information, documents or records demanded by an authorised officer within the time provided is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦200,000 in the first day of default and ₦10,000 for each subsequent day where the refusal continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 108]

If an extension of time to pay is granted and the person fails to pay within the extension, penalty and interest accrue from the due date of payment as if the extension was never granted. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The question does not say what kind of document the tax office sent (for example an assessment, a demand notice, or an information request), so one number of days cannot be given.
- For an information request or notice under section 108, the time allowed is not stated in these passages; it is described only as the time provided under this Act or any other tax law.
- The passages do not state the deadline for a return or for responding to other kinds of notice.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6) (gazette pages A 288, A 289)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65 (gazette pages A 298, A 299)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 108 (gazette pages A 313, A 314)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Interest is SOFR plus 10% or such other spread as the authority determines in the cited text; the National Assembly text says SOFR plus a spread to be determined, without the 10%. (DR-243)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Only the cited text makes the interest in subsection (1)(b) and (c) compound and applies it to tax debts unpaid at commencement. (DR-245)

cases.question: Where does the law say that company donations to charities can be deducted in full with no limit?

claims.text: The law does not say that company donations to charities are deductible in full with no limit. Section 164 does allow a company to deduct donations made for a period to a fund, body or institution in Nigeria to which the section applies.

The section applies to donations to public funds, statutory bodies or institutions, religious, charitable, educational and scientific institutions established in Nigeria, bodies recognised under the Diplomatic Immunities and Privileges Act, and any pandemic, natural disaster or other public emergency interventions.
The total deduction allowed to a company under this section for any year of assessment shall not exceed an amount equal to 10% of the profit before tax of that company for that year.
A company making a deduction for a donation shall provide requisite document evidencing the donation to the relevant tax authority.
For a donation other than in cash, the value for the purpose of this section is the lower of the market value at the time of the donation or the consideration paid for the item when it was acquired.

claims.text: A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on a taxable supply made to the person. That VAT is called input VAT.

A taxable person must, not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, remit the excess to the Service where output VAT exceeds input VAT.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.

Input tax on a taxable supply to a registered person may be deducted from the tax payable on its taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.

A taxable person must submit a VAT return on or before the 21st day of the following month. The return must show the input tax paid, output tax collected and VAT payable on all taxable supplies in the preceding month.
The rule that a taxable person files a VAT return by the 21st day does not apply to a small business.
A taxable person who is exempt as a small business is exempt from section 152 of the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025.

cases.rendered:
An expense incurred in a currency other than the Naira may only be deducted to the extent of its Naira equivalent at the official exchange rate published by the Central Bank of Nigeria for the relevant date or period. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(2) to (4)]

In ascertaining profits from a trade, business, profession or vocation, all expenses for the period wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of the income are deducted. This is subject to the exceptions in section 18 and Part IX of Chapter Two. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h)]

No deduction is allowed for any expense on which Value Added Tax is due under the Act but was not charged. For imported items, no deduction is allowed for any expense on which the applicable import duty or levy was not paid. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(p)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The conversion into naira is a calculation. It needs the Central Bank of Nigeria official exchange rate for the relevant date or period, which is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say whether an overseas advertising campaign is an expense wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of the income.
- The passages do not say whether Value Added Tax was due on this payment, or whether it was charged.
- Section 18 and Part IX of Chapter Two, which section 20(1) refers to, are not among the passages.
- The passages do not say which date or period is the relevant one for this payment.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(2) to (4) (gazette pages A 409, A 410)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h) (gazette pages A 408, A 409)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(p) (gazette page A 410)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(2) to (4): Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 193 of this Act; the National Assembly text cites section 194, which is gazette section 195. (DR-032)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h): Cross-reference: the gazette cites Part IX of Chapter Two (Rates of Tax), the National Assembly text Part XI (Specialised Trade or Business), which is the intended reference; the gazette reading is a printing slip (DQ-14). Cited as printed. The other difference ('in the course of' / 'during') is wording. (DR-029)

cases.question: Is there a time limit for asking for a VAT refund, and how quickly does the Service have to pay it?

claims.text: A taxable person that qualifies for a VAT refund shall make a request to the Service in the prescribed form.
The request shall be made not later than 12 months after the transaction giving rise to the refund, otherwise it shall lapse.

Where a valid request is received from a taxable person, the Service shall, not later than 30 days of receipt of the request, refund the tax to the taxable person or the amount shall be eligible for set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not utilised as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.

Separately, for tax refunds generally, no claim for refund of tax under that section is allowed unless it is made in writing within six years after the end of the year of assessment to which it relates.

Under that general refund section, any tax refund due shall be made within 90 days of the decision of the relevant tax authority made under subsection (2), with the option of a set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer.

gaps: The passages do not say how the general refund rules (six years and 90 days) relate to the specific VAT refund rules (12 months and 30 days), or which applies where they differ.

This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

This rule does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders. This is so whether the dividends are paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

This applies whether or not the recipient is a Nigerian company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

The company is charged at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend were the company's total profits for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent that the profits or gains in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

This rule does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders. This is so whether the dividends are paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 9]

- Any calculation of the tax on a particular dividend is not covered by the passages.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT.
A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom a taxable supply is made in Nigeria, and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remission shall be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service.
A foreign company means a non-resident company or any company other than a Nigerian company.

gaps: Whether software services are taxable supplies is not stated in the passages.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purposes of Chapter Two of the Act.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of the Nigerian company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation in that accounting period.
The deduction for interest on debt used to generate business income is subject to the Third Schedule.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Where interest expenditure is not wholly deducted for an assessment year, the part not deducted is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business it carries on for that year, to the extent permitted by paragraph (2) of the Schedule. It cannot be carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately after the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

For the Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.

All relevant facts are to be considered when computing the additional tax that should have been charged, even where those facts were not known when a prior assessment or additional assessment was made for the taxable person in the same year.
The provisions of the Act on notice of assessment, appeal and other proceedings apply to an assessment or additional assessment and to the tax charged.

claims.text: Section 192 deals with transactions between related parties, and its heading says they are to be at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length.
The company shall also report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party that is not at arm's length, the authority may make the necessary adjustments to bring it in line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations.
The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192.
For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions.
For section 192, "arm's length terms and conditions" means the terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances.
"Relevant tax authority" is in accordance with the provision of the Act and section 3 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.

Section 192 deals with transactions between related parties, and its heading says they are to be at arm's length. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

The company shall also report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party that is not at arm's length, the authority may make the necessary adjustments to bring it in line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations. The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of this Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.

Capital allowance is the amount relating to qualifying capital expenditure incurred in generating the assessable profits. It is prorated where an asset is only partly used to generate assessable profits, but it is not prorated where non-taxable income is less than 10% of the company's total income.

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

Where, in a year of assessment, a company's effective tax rate is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year.

gaps: The meaning of "small company" is not among the passages, so whether the company is taxed at 0% or 30 per cent cannot be determined.
The company's turnover, and whether it is part of an MNE group, are not stated, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies cannot be determined.
The question gives profit, not total profits after losses, capital allowances and other adjustments, so the taxable amount is not known.
